segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yes, and I ask you too, true companion, help these women, who struggled alongside me in the good news, together with Clement and the rest of my coworkers, whose names are in the book of life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let your gentleness be known to all people. The Lord is near.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, brothers and sisters, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is well spoken of—if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise—think about these things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What you learned and received and heard and saw in me—practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your concern for me has bloomed again; you were in fact concerned, but you had no opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that I say this out of want, for I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I know how to be brought low, and I know how to have more than enough. In anything and everything I have learned the secret—both to be well fed and to go hungry, both to have more than enough and to be in want.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have strength for everything in the one who empowers me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Still, you did well to share with me in my affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You Philippians yourselves also know that in the early days of the good news, when I left Macedonia, no assembly shared with me in an account of giving and receiving except you alone;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for even in Thessalonica you sent something for my need more than once.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that I seek the gift; rather, I seek the fruit that increases to your account.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have received payment in full and have more than enough. I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent—a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And my God will fill every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To our God and Father be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet every holy one in Christ Jesus. The brothers and sisters who are with me greet you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All the holy ones greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and the next verse speaks directly to two women in the community. “Brothers” alone would now suggest that only men are addressed. Many modern translations make the same choice; more literal ones keep “brothers” with a footnote.

The Greek word means someone yoked together with another, a partner or comrade. It may be a description of an unnamed colleague, or a proper name, Syzygus, with Paul playing on its meaning (“Syzygus, rightly so called”). The name is not attested elsewhere, so most translations take it as a description, but the identity of the person is unknown.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term or the name of a book, so the plain meaning is given here. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news”.

The Greek can mean near in time (the Lord’s coming is close, as in 3:20) or near in presence (the Lord is close to those who call on him, echoing the Psalms). Interpreters are divided, and Paul may intend both. The sentence can also be attached either to the call for gentleness before it or to the call not to be anxious after it.

The Greek word was a favorite term of Stoic and Cynic philosophers for the self-sufficiency of the wise person who needs nothing from outside. Paul borrows the term but relocates its source: verse 13 makes clear that his sufficiency comes from the one who empowers him, not from himself.

notes.traditional: I am instructed / I have learned the secret
notes.note: The verb, used only here in the New Testament, was the technical term for being initiated into the mystery religions. Paul uses it figuratively: his initiation has been into living with plenty and with hunger alike.

notes.phrase: I have strength for everything in the one who empowers me
notes.traditional: I can do all things through him who strengthens me
notes.note: The verb means to be strong or to have strength for something, and “everything” refers back to the circumstances just listed—plenty and hunger, abundance and want. The traditional wording is often heard as a promise of unlimited achievement; the context is endurance in every situation. Later manuscripts add “Christ” to identify the one who empowers, which is the reading behind the King James Version.

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and its reference is clear, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word.

notes.phrase: an account of giving and receiving
notes.traditional: in the matter of giving and receiving
notes.note: Paul uses the language of commerce throughout verses 15–18. “Account,” “giving and receiving” (credit and debit), “fruit” (which could also mean profit or interest), “increases,” and “received payment in full” (the wording of a receipt) were all familiar from business dealings. He describes the Philippians’ gifts as a partnership whose real profit accrues to them.

notes.traditional: an odour of a sweet smell / a fragrant offering
notes.note: This phrase is the Septuagint’s standard expression for the smell of a sacrifice rising to God and pleasing him, used from Genesis 8:21 onward and often in Leviticus. Paul moves from the language of the ledger to the language of the altar: the gift sent to him is really an offering to God.

The word is used of every member of the community as someone set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saint” now suggests a canonized individual or a person of exceptional virtue, which is not the meaning. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people”.

This does not mean the emperor’s relatives. The phrase covered the large body of slaves and freed slaves in the imperial service, who staffed the administration in Rome and in the provinces. Where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote is disputed (Rome is the traditional view; Ephesus and Caesarea are also proposed), and members of the imperial service were found in all of these places.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed communities recurs in every letter, and translators divide between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; readers would be confused by variation between chapters.

candidates.rendering: be of the same mind / concern
candidates.reason: A key Pauline verb (especially in Philippians and Romans) covering mindset, attitude and concern, where consistent English is hard and translators vary widely.
The κοινων- word family (share, partner, fellowship, participate) runs through Paul and Acts and needs one policy so that the partnership theme stays visible.
Frequent in Paul with renderings ranging from “abound” to “overflow” to “have plenty”; a single decision for the intransitive sense would keep the letters uniform.
Very common across the New Testament with senses of urge, appeal, encourage and comfort; the choice of English for each sense should be fixed across books.
